Amyraldianism
am-ih-RAL-dee-an-iz-um
noun (soteriology / historical theology)
Named for Moses Amyraut (1596-1664), a French Huguenot theologian of the Academy of Saumur, who taught a modified doctrine of the extent of the atonement sometimes called hypothetical universalism or the Saumur hypothesis, and more commonly Amyraldism or Amyraldianism.

Biblical Definition

Amyraldianism reorders the logical sequence of God’s eternal decrees regarding salvation. On the Amyraldian scheme, God first (in the order of logic, not of time) decrees to send Christ to die for all men without exception, conditioned on their faith — the atonement made universally sufficient and, in that sense, universally intended. Then, seeing by His foreknowledge that no fallen sinner would believe of his own will, God decrees a second, particular election, choosing some to whom He grants the effectual gift of faith. The system was devised to hold together universal-sounding texts (such as God’s desire that all men be saved) with the particular texts of election, without simply reading the universal texts as addressed to all kinds of men rather than every individual man, as the historic Reformed reading does. The doctrine was controversial within Reformed orthodoxy from its first appearance; the Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675) was drafted substantially to require subscription against it in the Swiss Reformed churches, on the ground that it introduces an unnecessary and unscriptural universal intention into the eternal decree, and risks becoming, in less careful hands, a halfway house toward a fuller Arminian scheme in which the human will, not God’s sovereign election, becomes the final deciding factor in who is actually saved.

Webster 1828 Definition

The theological system of Moses Amyraut, positing a universal but conditional divine intention in the atonement, followed by a particular election of those granted faith; rejected by the Reformed orthodox as compromising the doctrine of particular redemption.

AMYRALDIANISM, n. (soteriology / historical theology) The system of Moses Amyraut (1596-1664) of the Academy of Saumur.

Also called hypothetical universalism or the Saumur hypothesis.

Posits a logically prior universal, conditional divine intention in Christ’s death.

Followed by a particular election of those to whom saving faith is actually granted.

Answered by the Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675), which required subscription against it.

Key Scripture

Joh 10:11 — "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep."

Joh 10:15 — "As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep."

Eph 5:25 — "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;"

Mat 1:21 — "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins."

Modern Corruption

Amyraldianism softens particular redemption by inserting a logically prior universal intention into the atonement that Scripture does not require, and that the specific objects of Christ’s death named throughout the New Testament — His sheep, His church, His people — do not support.

expand to see more

Amyraldianism is the system that inserts, logically prior to God’s particular election, a universal and merely conditional divine intention in the atonement: Christ is said to have died for all men in a sense that secures nothing for anyone apart from a further, separately decreed gift of faith to the elect alone. The doctrine is a genuine attempt at reverence toward the whole counsel of Scripture, not a careless error, which is exactly why the Reformed churches judged it necessary to answer it formally rather than ignore it.

The Reformed answer is drawn from how Scripture itself describes the object of Christ’s death: not an undifferentiated mass of humanity but a specific, named people. The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep, not for the whole flock of the world indiscriminately (Joh 10:11, 15); Christ loved the church, and gave himself for it, a particular bride, not humanity in general (Eph 5:25); and He is named Jesus for this very reason, that he shall save his people from their sins — not merely make salvation possible for anyone who might believe, but actually save those given to Him (Mat 1:21). Particular redemption holds that Christ’s death actually and efficaciously secures the salvation of the elect, accomplishing precisely what it intends, rather than merely making salvation possible pending a further condition. The Amyraldian scheme, however carefully qualified, still locates the final decisive factor in whether a given sinner is granted faith, a second decree standing behind the first; the Reformed doctrine holds that election and redemption were never two decrees but one single, sovereign purpose, accomplishing from eternity exactly what it secures in time.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Named for Moses Amyraut of the Academy of Saumur, whose hypothetical-universalist scheme was formally answered by the Formula Consensus Helvetica of 1675.

expand to see more

Moses Amyraut (1596-1664) — French Huguenot theologian of the Academy of Saumur, the doctrine’s namesake.

Also called hypothetical universalism, naming the conditional, non-securing character of the universal intention.

Also called the Saumur hypothesis, after the French academy where it was taught.

Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675) — the Swiss Reformed confessional document drafted substantially to answer it.

Contrasted throughout Reformed orthodoxy with particular redemption, the doctrine that Christ’s death actually secures the salvation of the elect alone.

Usage

"Amyraldianism: the system of a logically prior universal, conditional atonement followed by particular election."

"Answered by the Formula Consensus Helvetica (1675) as a departure from particular redemption."

"Contrasted with the Reformed doctrine that Christ’s death actually and efficaciously secures the salvation of the elect."
